name: Broken Chair
label: Broken Chair
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Nations' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Nations' (way/1512168103): middle (293 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/846279674: the OpenStreetMap point 'Broken Chair'.
notes: Giant three-legged chair sculpture on Place des Nations.

text.description:
Broken Chair is a giant wooden chair with one leg snapped off halfway, and it is easy to read at a glance, even from across a busy square. Swiss artist Daniel Berset designed it and carpenter Louis Genève built it. It stands 12 metres high and uses 5.5 tonnes of wood. It stands across the street from the Palace of Nations and symbolises opposition to land mines and cluster bombs. Handicap International first put it up in August 1997, meant for three months. Strong public support kept it there until 2005, when the square was remodelled. It returned to the same place in February 2007.

It photographs well because the chair and the Palace of Nations can share one frame. That gives you a simple picture with a clear message: a huge, damaged piece of furniture in front of a seat of diplomacy. The best-known view is from the edge of the Place des Nations, facing the main gate. Step back far enough to keep the whole chair and its leg in the picture. If the fountain is running, the jets can add a foreground, but it only runs in warmer months and when switched on, so don't count on it. The square is open and windswept, with traffic around it, and it is sometimes used for protests, which can bring banners or crowds into your shot. For a different picture, go right up to the chair and shoot steeply upwards at the shortened leg, which shows the scale well.
text.geographic_location: It stands on the Place des Nations in Geneva, across the street from the Palace of Nations and in front of its main entrance.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach the Place des Nations opposite the Palace of Nations. From there the chair is to the north-east, so you can also walk up for the close-up view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand, so the chair and the palace gates look natural together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and want the whole chair in the frame. If you are far back, the telephoto (2x or more) can crop in on the chair and the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Nations (edge of the square facing the main UN gate). The whole chair in the foreground with the Palais des Nations and its gates behind it, with the fountain jets optionally in the foreground. Adjust your position only if the chair looks too small or too large in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the chair's legs against the vertical lines, with the phone held level so the chair does not lean. Put the chair slightly off-centre and let the palace fill the space beside it. For a second picture, walk up to the chair and tilt the phone upwards at the shortened leg, or shoot from across the square for a wide view that shows how big the monument is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the chair to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the wood keeps its detail. If you are close, the ultra-wide (0.5x) can stretch and bend the edges, so keep the chair away from the corners of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when fewer people walk through the frame.

text.access_note: The chair stands in an open public square; the palace grounds are tied to the UN site and guided visits, so check the official site before you go if you want to photograph from the palace steps.

name: Jet d'Eau
label: Jet d'Eau
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/60018172: the OpenStreetMap point 'Jet d'eau'.
notes: Famous lake fountain shooting water about 140 m high.

text.description: The Jet d'Eau is a huge fountain at the point where Lake Geneva exits as the Rhône, and it is one of Geneva's best-known landmarks. It shoots about 500 litres of water every second up to 150 metres, leaving the nozzle at around 200 km/h. It is easy to photograph because the white column stands alone against the sky and the lake, with nothing else competing for attention. The present fountain dates from 1951, and the jet has stood at this spot since 1891. The first one, in 1886, reached only about 30 metres. You walk out to it along a stone jetty from the left bank of the lake, which puts you very close to the base. The fountain runs by day all year, except in frost or very strong wind. From spring to autumn it also runs in the evening, lit by 21 lights. Keep a dry cloth handy for your phone lens. Check the official site before you go if you are hoping to see it running.
text.geographic_location: The Jet d'Eau stands at the point where Lake Geneva exits as the Rhône, reached via a stone jetty from the left bank of the lake.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the left bank of the lake in central Geneva and follow the stone jetty on foot towards the fountain. Continue along the jetty and stand at the phone icon on the map. From there the jet is about 18 metres to the south-west. You can see the jet from far across the city, so it works as a landmark to head towards. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) at this distance, because the jet is very tall and you are close. The default lens (1x) works for a tighter shot of the spray at the base or the top of the column. The telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for details of the plume against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. The fountain is directly in front of you and the lake spreads out behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright (portrait) so the full height of the column fits, and tilt the phone up slowly rather than stepping back. Switch on gridlines and place the jet along one vertical line, with a little lake or sky either side. For a different view, turn round and frame the jet from a longer distance along the jetty or lakeshore.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white column to set focus and pull the exposure slider down a little so the bright water keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo or motion capture to catch the spray falling. Wipe the lens often, as it picks up mist quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: In the evening from spring to autumn, when the fountain is lit; use night mode and hold the phone steady against the rail or your body. By day, check the wind before you go, since a change in direction can soak the jetty.

text.access_note: The jetty is part of an open public waterside area, but the fountain can be switched off in frost or strong wind, so check the official site before you go.

name: Flower Clock
label: Flower Clock
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardin Anglais' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardin Anglais' (way/4272831): middle (411 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6228932679: the OpenStreetMap point 'Flower clock'.
notes: Floral clock in the Jardin Anglais.

text.description:
The Flower Clock (L'horloge fleurie) is a working clock set into the lawn at the western side of the Jardin Anglais, beside Lake Geneva. It was created in 1955 as a nod to the city's watchmakers and to nature. The dial is about 5 metres across and is planted with around 6,500 flowering plants and shrubs. The planting is changed with the seasons, so the picture is different each time you visit. Winter displays are generally less colourful than the rest of the year. The second hand is 2.5 metres long, said to be the longest in the world.

It photographs well because it gives you bright colour, a clear round shape and a lake backdrop all in one place. There are two good ways to shoot it. Close to the dial, you can fill the foreground with the flowers and the hands and keep the lake and open sky behind. From the tree-lined garden paths at the west end of the park, you can step back and frame the clock with mature trees, with the lake and the Jet d'Eau far off in the distance. This second view is quieter and works well for a wider scene. Summer afternoons bring tour groups around the dial, so be patient and wait for a gap. Keep your phone low and a little in front of the dial rather than looking straight down at it, so the flowers and the water both fit in.
text.geographic_location: The Flower Clock is in the Jardin Anglais, the lakeside park in central Geneva, on its western side near the Quai du Général-Guisan. The park runs along the water's edge, so the lake is right beside you.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the lakefront in central Geneva and make your way to the west end of the Jardin Anglais, by the Quai du Général-Guisan. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the dial with the lake behind. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close and want the whole dial and the sky in one frame. If you stay on the paths, try 2x telephoto to pull the clock in without walking into the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardin Anglais (west end, by the Quai du Général-Guisan, on the garden paths). The clock seen from the tree-lined garden paths, with the lake and the Jet d'Eau in the distance. You see the clock among mature trees, with the lake and the Jet d'Eau in the distance. For a closer, more graphic shot, walk over to the dial itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the paths, use the trees as a natural frame on one side and keep the clock in the lower third, with the lake above it. Switch on the gridlines to keep the horizon level. As an alternative, from right beside the dial you can put the flowers and hands in the foreground and the lake and open sky behind them. Crouch slightly to bring the flowers up in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dial to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch if the sky is bright, so the flower colours stay rich. Try a short Live Photo if the second hand is in view, and keep portrait mode for people rather than the clock.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the dial is not surrounded by visitors. Summer afternoons are busy with tour groups. The lakeside is often recommended for sunset photos, so a late-day visit can combine the clock with a warm sky. Flowers look best in the warmer months, when the planting is fuller.

text.access_note: The clock stands in an open public park, so you can walk up to it freely, but check the official Geneva city site before you go for any changes.
claims_not_in_sources: Summer afternoons are busy with tour groups, so other times of day are likely to be quieter.
The lakeside area is often recommended for sunset photos.
The flower display is fuller and more colourful in the warmer months than in winter.
The Jet d'Eau can be seen in the distance from the garden paths near the clock.
The clock is roughly a minute's walk from the stand-here point.

name: Palace of Nations
label: Palace of Nations
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place des Nations' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place des Nations' (way/1512168103): middle (293 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q594846: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Palace of Nations is the Geneva home of the United Nations, and it began life as the headquarters of the League of Nations. It was built between 1929 and 1938 by five architects who combined their ideas after a competition with 377 entries. When it was completed in 1936, it was the second-largest building complex in Europe by volume, behind only Versailles. With later extensions the complex is about 600 metres long. It stands in Ariana Park, which Gustave de Revilliod de la Rive left to the city in 1890 on condition that it stays open to the public.

The building is mostly hidden behind a security wall and trees, so the best street-level view is from Place des Nations. From there you see the main entrance and façade framed by the row of member-state flags. The giant Broken Chair sculpture stands in the foreground, which makes an easy way to show scale and give the photo a clear subject. If you have time, Parc de l'Ariana is a good alternative. It shows the Palace across the gardens, with fountains, sculptures and Lake Geneva behind.

Keep your phone level so the long façade does not lean. Let the flags and the chair fill the foreground, then step a little to either side until the entrance sits neatly between them. The Palace is a working diplomatic site, so stay on the public side of the barriers and follow any signs about photography.
text.geographic_location: The Palace of Nations stands in Ariana Park, in Geneva, overlooking Lake Geneva.
text.directions_text: Walk north towards the flags and the Broken Chair to reach the Place des Nations view on the south side of the Palace's approach, and the main entrance is straight ahead. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the flags, the façade and the Broken Chair together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to stand close to the sculpture and make it look large. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the entrance between the flags.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place des Nations (south side, facing the main entrance across the approach). The Palace's main entrance and façade framed by the row of member-state flags, with the giant Broken Chair sculpture in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the façade with the horizontal lines so the building looks straight. Put the Broken Chair low in the frame and the flags and entrance behind it. For a different view, Parc de l'Ariana shows the Palace across the gardens with Lake Geneva behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Take a few shots with people walking past the sculpture to show scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is high enough to light the façade from behind you, such as the middle of the day or the afternoon.

text.access_note: The Palace sits behind a security perimeter, so photograph from the public square and check the official site before you go for visits and any photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Because you face north from Place des Nations, the sun is behind you and lights the façade around midday and in the afternoon.
Place des Nations is open to the public for photography from the street side.

name: Reformation Wall
label: Reformation Wall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parc des Bastions' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parc des Bastions' (way/5073078): middle (498 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/36174871: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mur des réformateurs'.
notes: Monument to Calvin, Farel, Beza and Knox in Parc des Bastions.

text.description: The Reformation Wall is a long stone monument set into Geneva's old city walls, opened in 1909 to mark 400 years since John Calvin's birth and 350 years since the University of Geneva was founded. Four statues, each 5 metres tall, stand at the centre: Farel, Calvin, Beza and Knox. Smaller 3-metre figures stand on either side, and the Latin motto Post Tenebras Lux (After darkness, light) is carved along the wall. From the park the whole wall, about 100 metres long, fits in one photo, with the pond in front and the old trees around it. That makes it an easy, rewarding subject for a phone. Take the wide view first, then move closer for the statues, whose carved faces and lettering look good in a tighter frame. In spring and autumn the park's mature trees add colour behind the stonework. Late afternoon usually gives the kindest light on the statues. The wall is lit at night, so it can also work after dark if you hold the phone steady. Give yourself a few minutes to walk along the front, because the wall looks quite different from the centre and from either end.
text.geographic_location: The wall stands in the Parc des Bastions, in the grounds of the University of Geneva, built into the old city walls.
text.directions_text: Head for the Parc des Bastions and the University of Geneva grounds. The wall is to the north-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole wall. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the trees and pond. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the four central statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parc des Bastions (the broad forecourt directly in front of the wall, with the pond between you and the statues). The whole 100-metre wall with the four central 5-metre statues of Farel, Calvin, Beza and Knox, framed by the park's old trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the top of the wall level with a horizontal line so the stonework doesn't look tilted. Leave a strip of trees at the top and the pond at the bottom. If you want a different view, walk along the paths of the Promenade des Bastions for the wall seen through the greenery, with the statues against the old fortification. Just look for a gap in the foliage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone of the wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and bright stone don't wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something firm, or keep the phone still for the full capture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives warmer side light on the statues. Late-morning sun falls full on the faces and is harsher. Spring and autumn add colour in the trees behind. The wall is also lit at night.

text.access_note: The wall is in a public park, but check the official site before you go for any park opening times or restrictions.

name: Jardin Anglais
label: Jardin Anglais
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Horloge Fleurie' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Horloge fleurie' (node/6228932679): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1083364: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Lakeside park at the Pont du Mont-Blanc.

text.description: The Jardin Anglais is a city park on Geneva's lakefront, laid out in 1855 on the site of an old harbour and a wood. It marks the start of the Quai Gustave-Ador. When the Pont du Mont-Blanc was built in 1863, the park took its present shape, a trapezoid of about 25,430 square metres. Its best-known feature is the Horloge Fleurie, the flower clock. The clock face sits on a sloping bed of flowers, so it reads clearly from the pavement. Behind it you get the lakefront quay and the garden. The park also holds the national monument, several pavilions, a bronze fountain by Alexis André and a coffeehouse, and it hosts Geneva's annual Christmas Market. For a postcard-style picture, stand on the pavement in front of the clock, a little to one side of the crowds, on the Quai du Général-Guisan side. Fit the whole flower face in the lower part of the frame and let some trees and the quay fill the rest. Early morning or late afternoon is calmer, and the light is softer. The clock stands beside a busy road, so a tight shot may keep traffic out. If you have time, the Monument national and the Fontaine des Quatre-Saisons also make good pictures, and both are worth a short wander.
text.geographic_location: The Jardin Anglais is in central Geneva, on the lakefront, at the start of the Quai Gustave-Ador.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so head for the lakefront in central Geneva, at the start of the Quai Gustave-Ador, and look for the Jardin Anglais. Look for the flower clock on the pavement beside the quay. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the flower clock and the quay behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more trees and sky, and keep the clock away from the edges so it does not stretch. Use telephoto (2x or more) for a tight shot of the clock face that leaves out passing traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (pavement in front of the clock, a little to one side of the crowds, on the Quai du Général-Guisan side). The flower clock face on its sloping bed in the foreground, with the lakefront quay and the garden behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the clock face on the lower third, with the quay and the garden above it. For a wider picture, include some of the trees. If you want a different subject, the Monument national (two bronze figures above a round red flower bed) or the Fontaine des Quatre-Saisons (framed by the trees) are good alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clock face to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the flower colours stay rich. Take a few frames, since people and traffic keep moving past.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, before the tour groups arrive and when the light is softer. The flowers look best in daylight.

text.access_note: The garden is a public park and, as far as we know, open around the clock, but check the official site before you go, especially during events such as the Christmas Market.

name: St. Pierre Cathedral
label: St. Pierre Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue Etienne-Dumont' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rue Etienne-Dumont nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/397737238: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Pierre Cathedral' (94 m across).
notes: Calvin's church in the old town with a tower view.

text.description:
St. Pierre Cathedral stands on the hill at the heart of Geneva's Old Town. Its towers and green spire are easy to pick out above the surrounding rooftops. It has been the principal church of the Protestant Church of Geneva since 1535 and is closely linked with John Calvin, who preached here. The present building was begun around 1160 in the Gothic style. The classical portico on the front was added in the 18th century, so you get a medieval church with a Neo-Classical face. Below the cathedral there is an archaeological site, a reminder of how long people have used this hill.

For a phone photo, the best approach is the old street view. The area near Rue Etienne-Dumont and Place du Bourg-de-Four gives a close, street-level look at the cathedral from the Old Town. If you want the wider skyline, the Pont du Mont-Blanc shows the towers and green spire above the Old Town across the lake. The Cour de Saint-Pierre, the courtyard in front, is the place for the portico. Take your time, as the streets here are for walking and other visitors will be passing. Check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside or climb a tower.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town (Vieille Ville) of Geneva, near Place du Bourg-de-Four. The cathedral is the large landmark in the middle of the district.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is listed for this spot, so walk from Place du Bourg-de-Four in the Old Town. From there the cathedral is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the cathedral from the street. If the street is too narrow to fit the towers in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the spire or the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue Etienne-Dumont. A close, street-level view of the cathedral from the Old Town near Place du Bourg-de-Four.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the cathedral as the main subject and leave a little of the street around it to give a sense of place. Turn on gridlines and keep the towers upright by holding the phone level, and tilt it up only a little. For other views, try the Pont du Mont-Blanc for the towers and green spire above the skyline across the lake, or the Cour de Saint-Pierre for the portico.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the stone keeps its detail. Take a few shots at different zoom levels so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the stonework than the harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The street and the courtyard are public places, but the cathedral is a working church and the tower climb is paid, so check the official site before you go for access details.

name: Place du Bourg-de-Four
label: Bourg-de-Four
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place du Bourg-de-Four' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place du Bourg-de-Four' (way/1511645040): middle (200 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1511645040: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Place du Bourg-de-Four' (201 m across).
notes: Oldest square in Geneva's old town.

text.description: Place du Bourg-de-Four is a cobbled square in the heart of Geneva's Old Town. It sits on the site of the old Roman forum and medieval market, and in the 19th century it was a stagecoach stop. Today it is a popular meeting place, with restaurants and cafes around a small marble fountain from the 18th century. It photographs well because everything you want is in one frame. The fountain makes a natural foreground, and the tall 16th to 18th century houses and cafe terraces rise behind it. The cobbles and the mix of building fronts give the picture a lived-in, old-town feel. The best-known view is from beside the central fountain, looking uphill, with the fountain close to the lens and the houses stacked behind. For a second picture, turn towards the northern row of old townhouses and cafes. The twin towers of Saint-Pierre Cathedral show above the roofs there. A wider view across the lower part of the square, with its buildings, people and cafes, gives a good sense of the place. In good weather the cafe terraces fill up and can block the fountain, so you may need to wait a moment or shift a step or two to keep it clear. Late morning gives sun without the lunch crowd, and late afternoon is also recommended.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Geneva, close to Saint-Pierre Cathedral. It is a pedestrian-feeling square with restaurants and cafes all around it.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot. The square is in the Old Town near Saint-Pierre Cathedral, so head for the Old Town and then for the cathedral; the square is close by. Once you are on the square, look for the small marble fountain on the ground. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain-and-houses view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wide view across the lower part of the square. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cathedral towers above the northern row of houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place du Bourg-de-Four (by the central fountain, looking uphill). The fountain in the foreground with the tall old houses and cafe terraces of the square rising behind it. Then move to the fountain and look uphill.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the fountain low in the frame and let the houses fill the rest. Turn on the gridlines and line the fountain up on one of the lower crossing points. Hold the phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a different picture, turn to the northern row of townhouses and cafes and use the telephoto lens to frame the cathedral towers behind them. The ultra-wide (0.5x) works for the broad view across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or pale stone looks washed out. If people walk through the frame, try a Live Photo and pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is recommended by one guide. Late morning gives sun without the lunch crowd. Cafe terraces are busy in good weather and may block the fountain.

text.access_note: It is an open public square that you can walk into and photograph from.

name: Brunswick Monument
label: Brunswick Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardin des Alpes' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardin des Alpes' (way/666867599): middle (157 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/666867576: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Monument Brunswick' (15 m across).
notes: Neo-Gothic mausoleum on the lake shore.

text.description: The Brunswick Monument is a white marble tomb in the Jardin des Alpes, on the Geneva lakefront. It was built for Charles II, Duke of Brunswick, who left his fortune to the city on condition that it raise him a grand monument modelled on the Scaliger Tombs in Verona. It was unveiled on 14 October 1879. The monument has three storeys and a hexagonal canopy over a figure of the duke lying on his sarcophagus. Marble statues stand at the corners, and chimeras and lions guard the platform, which is 65 metres long and 25 metres wide. Part of the duke's legacy also paid for the Grand Théâtre. It photographs well because the pale, detailed spire stands out against the trees and sky, and the lake lies just beyond. The classic picture is taken from across the park. The interior is generally closed, so plan on photographing it from outside. If you want a wider scene with more water, the Quai du Mont-Blanc promenade and the Jardin Anglais are good alternatives.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands in the Jardin des Alpes on the Quai du Mont-Blanc, close to the waterfront promenade on Lake Geneva.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Quai du Mont-Blanc on the lakefront. The Jardin des Alpes sits right on that waterfront. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the monument with the fountain behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to take in the whole platform and the lawns. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the spire and statues, and to bring the Jet d'Eau closer behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardin des Alpes (across the park from the monument, facing it with the lake behind the Jet d'Eau). The neo-Gothic monument in the foreground with the Jet d'Eau fountain rising in the distance over Lake Geneva. Step back across the lawns until the spire and the fountain sit together in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the spire on one vertical line, with the fountain and lake above the horizon line in the background. Keep the phone level so the monument does not lean. For a different version, take a wider shot from the Quai du Mont-Blanc promenade, or from the Jardin Anglais with the lake filling the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white marble to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the stone keeps its detail rather than turning flat white. Portrait mode is not needed for this view; the 2x or 3x zoom works better for close-ups of the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. One guide also suggests sunset.

text.access_note: The monument stands in a public park and is photographed from outside, as the interior is generally closed; check for seasonal works along the lakeside paths before you go.

name: Geneva Botanical Garden
label: Botanical Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardin botanique de Genève' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardin botanique de Genève' (relation/8224276): edge nearest the subject (891 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8224276: large area 'Geneva Botanic Garden' (895 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large garden near the lake and the UN.

text.description: Geneva Botanical Garden is a large, calm park of lawns, mature trees and glasshouses on the north side of the city, beside Lake Geneva and the United Nations park. It was founded in 1817 by Augustin Pyramus de Candolle and now covers 28 hectares. About 700,000 visits were recorded in 2023, which made it the city's most visited attraction. For photos, the best-known subject is the domed temperate glasshouse. Its glass-and-iron frame is surrounded by palms and trees and looks good across an open stretch of lawn. The garden's greenhouses are glass and iron in the style fashionable in the later 19th century, so the lines and curves are easy to use in a phone frame. Inside, a gallery lets you look down on the planting, which is worth a few shots if it is open to you. Elsewhere in the garden, Villa Le Chêne, the reception building, makes a gentle composition of lawn, old trees and house. The rock garden, with alpine-style planting beside a small pond, suits closer, more detailed pictures. The whole garden, including the greenhouses and the two mansions, is registered as a cultural asset of national importance. Take your time here: the glasshouse and the lawns reward a slow walk and a few different angles.
text.geographic_location: In northern Geneva, beside Lake Geneva and next to the park of the United Nations Office at Geneva. The garden's Console site is at 192 rue de Lausanne.
text.directions_text: Head from central Geneva towards the lakeside and the United Nations park and look for the garden next to it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole glasshouse and the lawn in front of it. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and foreground, but keep the dome central so the edges do not stretch. Telephoto (2x-5x) is good for the dome and the palms close to the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (domed temperate glasshouse, exterior view across the lawn). The glass-and-dome temperate glasshouse with palms and trees around it, the garden's most-photographed building. From here the domed temperate glasshouse lies to the west, across the lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome slightly off-centre, with the lawn filling the lower third. Keep the vertical lines of the glasshouse straight by holding the phone level. For an alternative, try Villa Le Chêne behind its lawn and mature trees, or the rock garden beside its small pond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glasshouse to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright glass and sky keep their detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the glass and the planting. Overcast days also cut glare on the glass.

text.access_note: The garden is a public visitor attraction; check the official site before you go for opening times, any closures and whether the glasshouse gallery needs a separate ticket.

name: Pont du Mont-Blanc
label: Pont du Mont-Blanc
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quai du Mont-Blanc' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Quai du Mont-Blanc nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8718609: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pont du Mont-Blanc' (294 m across).
notes: Bridge over the Rhône at the lake outlet.

text.description:
The Pont du Mont-Blanc is a major bridge in the middle of Geneva. It carries the main north–south road across the water and has done so since it was inaugurated in 1862. It is about 250 metres long and takes its name from Mont Blanc, the highest massif in the Alps, which can be seen from the city on a clear day. The bridge also marks the point where Lake Geneva's harbour (the Rade de Genève) turns into the Rhône. A few metres to the west, in the river, lies the little Ile Rousseau.

The best photo is from Quai du Mont-Blanc, the lakeside promenade, looking across at the bridge. The bridge sits in the frame with the lake quay, the Jet d'Eau and the waterfront buildings around it. If you have time for a second angle, the Monument de Brunswick in the lakeside gardens gives a good view of the Jet d'Eau and the harbour with the bridge nearby. Quai des Bergues offers a low, close-up view of the arch and underside.

Traffic is heavy and the area gets busy at peak times. Cyclists are sometimes pushed onto the pavement, so keep clear of them when you set up. The Jet d'Eau is not always running, and Mont Blanc only shows on clear days, so treat both as a bonus.
text.geographic_location: In central Geneva, where Lake Geneva narrows into the Rhône, linking the left and right banks. The viewpoint is on the lakeside Quai du Mont-Blanc, next to the bridge.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so check a local journey planner for the best way to reach the lakefront at the Rade de Genève in central Geneva. It is about 2 minutes on foot from the middle of the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the bridge, the quay and the lake in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the bridge with the city behind it. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the Jet d'Eau or the mountains in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Quai du Mont-Blanc (lakeside promenade, looking across at the bridge). The bridge spanning the Rhône in the frame, with the lake quay, the Jet d'Eau and the city's waterfront architecture around it. The bridge lies to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up along a lower third, with the water in the foreground and the city behind. Keep the horizon level, as the long bridge shows up any tilt. For a different view, try the lakeside gardens by the Monument de Brunswick, or a low angle on the arch from Quai des Bergues.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the sky to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the water and sky from washing out. Wipe the lens first, as lake spray and fingerprints cause haze. Keep a short burst or Live Photo going to catch a gap in the traffic or people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light on the mountains is best. Mont Blanc is only visible on clear days.

text.access_note: The quay is an open public promenade, but check the official site before you go if you plan to use any other viewpoint or event area nearby.
claims_not_in_sources: Quai du Mont-Blanc is an open public lakeside promenade that anyone can walk along.
The 0.5x ultra-wide lens is wide enough to fit the bridge, the quay and the lake in one frame from the viewpoint.
Lens spray and fingerprints can cause haze on a phone camera near water.

name: International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum
label: Red Cross Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/189088527: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'ICRC' (106 m across).

text.description:
The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum is in Geneva, right beside the headquarters of the International Committee of the Red Cross. It opened in 1988. Wide, calm photos of the buildings and the open space around them are a good thing to aim for here.

Inside, the collection holds about 30,000 items. One of them is the first Nobel Peace Prize medal, awarded jointly in 1901 to Henry Dunant, who founded the Red Cross, and the French pacifist Frédéric Passy. The museum also holds the archives of the International Prisoners of War Agency, which UNESCO has listed in its Memory of the World Register for helping to reconnect people separated during the First World War. It welcomes around 120,000 visitors a year, so the building is well used.

For your photos, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the outline of the neighbouring International Committee of the Red Cross headquarters, right beside the museum. From there, walk a little way and turn to face the museum to choose your view. Switch on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight, because tilting the phone upwards makes tall walls lean inwards. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then move closer for a tighter picture of an entrance, a sign or the flags. Check for reflections in glass before you press the shutter. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go, since interior photography rules are not covered here.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Geneva, Switzerland, right next to the headquarters of the International Committee of the Red Cross.
text.directions_text: Start from central Geneva and head for the museum next to the International Committee of the Red Cross headquarters. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the headquarters outline, next to the museum, so walk a little way and turn to face the museum to choose your view. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views of the buildings. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit more of the buildings into one frame. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as signs, flags and entrances.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The museum is next door, so walk a little way and turn to face it. For a full view of a building, walk a little way back from it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of walls with them so that the buildings do not lean. Keep the phone level and at chest height. Take one wide shot to show the whole setting, then a tighter 2x shot of a single detail. Include a person for scale, if one happens to be there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so that the sky and pale surfaces keep their detail. If glass causes reflections, shift a step to one side and try again.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, such as a bright overcast day or the morning or late afternoon, usually gives the most even results on large buildings.

text.access_note: The museum is a visitor attraction that may have ticketed entry and set hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes tall walls appear to lean inwards (general photography advice).
Soft daylight such as overcast conditions or the morning or late afternoon usually gives even results on large buildings.
Glass surfaces near the buildings may cause reflections in photos.
Museum entry may be ticketed and interior photography rules may apply; visitors should check the official site.

sources.title: International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum

name: Bâtiment des Forces motrices
label: Forces motrices
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pont de la Coulouvrenière' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pont de la Coulouvrenière' (way/82823135): middle (163 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/15257130: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bâtiment des Forces Motrices' (155 m across).
notes: Historic hydroelectric building on the Rhône.

text.description:
The Bâtiment des Forces motrices sits on an island in the Rhône, close to where the river leaves Lake Geneva. It was built between 1883 and 1892 as the power house of a hydro plant and waterworks. Its job was to use the river's flow to supply water pressure to the city's drinking water and to local workshops, including watchmakers. It stopped working as a power source in 1963 and reopened in 1997 as an opera house and concert hall. Today it is a good subject for a phone because the neo-classical stone building, with its tall round-arched windows, rises straight out of the water.

From there the riverside façade is framed by the bridge, with the Rhône flowing below. The building looks best in the evening or at blue hour, when it is lit up. If you want a wider view with neighbouring buildings in the frame, the platform of the Barrage du Seujet, just downstream, gives a second angle across the river.

The building is usually open to visitors only on event nights, so treat the exterior as your main photo and don't plan on getting inside. Keep your phone away from the railing edge, and watch for passing cyclists and pedestrians while you frame the shot.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Geneva, on an island in the Rhône just below the point where the river flows out of Lake Geneva. It stands beside the Pont de la Coulouvrenière and the Seujet dam.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot. Head to the Rhône and the Pont de la Coulouvrenière on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole façade and the bridge fit in the frame. Then try 2x-3x zoom if your phone has it, to pick out the arched windows and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pont de la Coulouvrenière. The building's riverside façade rising out of the Rhône, framed by the bridge, which is the setting most photographers use for the exterior.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the building along the lower or upper third, with the river in the foreground. Try the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to include more of the bridge, but keep the building away from the edges so it doesn't stretch. For a wider alternative with neighbouring buildings in view, try the platform of the Barrage du Seujet downstream.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit windows don't burn out. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone still against the bridge railing or your body while it takes the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening or blue hour, when the building is lit and the façade looks especially good in the evening light.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the bridge, but the building itself is usually open only on event nights, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Grand Théâtre de Genève
label: Grand Théâtre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Place de Neuve' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Place Neuve' (way/1513907815): middle (205 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/15256736: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Grand Théâtre de Genève' (114 m across).
notes: Neoclassical opera house on Place de Neuve.

text.description:
The Grand Théâtre is Geneva's opera house, and the main facade is the part most visitors photograph. It looks across Place de Neuve in a grand Second Empire style, borrowed in part from the Palais Garnier in Paris. Eight large limestone pillars alternate with six smaller red granite ones. Marble statues of Drama, Dance, Music and Comedy balance the central facade, and a pediment with Geneva's coat of arms tops the building. The theatre was inaugurated in 1879 with Rossini's William Tell. A fire in 1951 destroyed the stage and auditorium, but the facades survived. It reopened in 1962 and still has the largest stage in Switzerland.

The photo works because the square gives you room to step back and fit the whole front into one frame. General Dufour's equestrian statue stands in the foreground, with the opera house rising behind it. Keep the statue to one side or low in the frame so it adds depth without hiding the entrance. Then zoom in for details such as the sculptures and the busts of composers under the roofline. The Parc des Bastions gives a second view of the theatre from the park side, framed by trees. The auditorium and grand staircase are indoors, so a performance or tour ticket is needed to photograph them.
text.geographic_location: The theatre stands on Place Neuve, between the Musée Rath and the Conservatory of Music. The site was once part of the moat of the old city wall.
text.directions_text: Head to Place de Neuve. Once you are the theatre is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. Walk across the square towards the main facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole facade and the statue in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and the building will not fit. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pediment, the sculptures and the busts under the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Place de Neuve (across the square from the main facade). The theatre's facade across the square, with General Dufour's equestrian statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the facade's vertical edges up with them, so the building does not lean. Put the statue slightly off-centre so the entrance stays visible behind it. For a different view, try the Parc des Bastions side, where the park entrance and trees frame the theatre. Check the exact spot on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface while it captures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour suits the exterior. Evening is good for the lit facade.

text.access_note: Place de Neuve is a public, open-air square with no ticket needed, but the interior needs a performance or tour ticket, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep the vertical edges of a building straight in a phone photo.
Holding a phone steady against your body or a solid surface helps in night mode.
The ultra-wide lens may be needed if you are close to the building and it does not fit in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider can keep detail in the stonework when the sky is bright.

name: Musée d'Art et d'Histoire
label: Art and History Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Promenade de l'Observatoire' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Promenade de l'Observatoire' (way/5172832): middle (194 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1289171: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Musée d'Art et d'Histoire' (133 m across).
notes: Large museum of art and archaeology.

text.description:
The Musée d'Art et d'Histoire holds one of the largest museum collections in Switzerland, with more than 650,000 objects covering archaeology, applied arts, watchmaking and fine art. The building is as photogenic as anything inside it. Marc Camoletti designed it, and it was built between 1903 and 1910 with money left by the banker Charles Galland. It is a square block with sides of about 60 m around an inner courtyard, four storeys high, with a triangular gable over the entrance. Sculptures by Paul Amlehn decorate the front, and the upper frieze carries the names of Genevan artists. Since 2021 the facade has also carried a digital countdown clock by the artist Gianni Motti, which may show up in your frame.

A photo guide also recommends the Promenade de l'Observatoire, facing the museum across the small park, and rates this as a top Geneva photo location, but warns that the big facade is hard to shoot well. Treat it as a patient shot: step back, keep the building straight, and give the gable some space above it. With the right angle, the Jet d'Eau can be framed between the buildings nearby, which makes a good second picture. If you want a different view, walk to Rue Charles-Galland for the north and east facades.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Les Tranchées, in Geneva's city centre, on the site of the former fortification ring. The Promenade de l'Observatoire is the small park facing it.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for Les Tranchées in the city centre. From there the museum is to the south-west, about 2 minutes on foot. A photo guide also recommends the Promenade de l'Observatoire, the small park facing the museum, if you want to compare views. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if trees or railings force you too close. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the sculptures on the gable and for the Jet d'Eau between the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Promenade de l'Observatoire (facing the museum across the small park). The museum's large front facade across the park, and at the right angle, the Jet d'Eau framed between the buildings. Move a little left or right until the Jet d'Eau appears between the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them, so the facade doesn't lean. Leave a little sky above the gable. Take one wide shot of the full facade, then a zoomed shot of the Jet d'Eau between the buildings. For a different view, Rue Charles-Galland shows the museum's north and east facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework. If you are shooting at dusk or after dark, try night mode and hold the phone against a post or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the facade is evenly lit, such as a bright overcast day or soft evening light. If you happen to catch a light show projected on the building, a night shot can be very rewarding, but I can't confirm any show is on, so treat it as a bonus.

text.access_note: The park is open public space; if you want to go inside the museum, check the official site before you go.

name: Pierres du Niton
label: Pierres du Niton
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jardin Anglais' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jardin Anglais' (way/4272831): middle (411 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/25648489: the OpenStreetMap point 'Pierre du Niton'.
notes: Erratic boulders used as the Swiss survey reference point.

text.description:
The Pierres du Niton are two big granite boulders standing in the water of Geneva's harbour. They were left here by the Rhone glacier at the end of the last ice age. The larger one, further from the shore, is called the Repère, and it has a place in Swiss map-making. In the 19th century Guillaume-Henri Dufour used it as the height starting point for his maps, and it is still the reference for height measurement in Switzerland. The name Niton comes from Neptune, the water god. Square holes in the top of the larger stone, noticed in 1660, may have been cut in the Bronze Age.

The stones photograph well because they sit alone in open water, with the lake and moored boats behind them. That gives you a simple, uncluttered picture. They are small in the frame from the shore, so go for a calm, tidy composition rather than a big dramatic one. Take one wider shot with the default lens (1x) to show the setting, then zoom in for a closer picture of the rocks. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines. Swimming is not allowed in this part of the lake, so enjoy them from the shore.
text.geographic_location: The stones lie in Geneva harbour, off the left bank of the lake near Quai Gustave-Ador. The Jardin Anglais, the lakeside park in the city centre, is the main place to view them from.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Jardin Anglais on the lakeside in central Geneva. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto setting (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the stones themselves, as they sit out in open water. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a wider picture with the lake and boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jardin Anglais (lakeside edge of the park, looking out over the harbour toward the stones). The two granite boulders standing out of the harbour water, with the lake and moored boats behind them. Look out over the harbour to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the larger stone on one of the lines, with the horizon on the lower or upper line. Leave some empty water around the rocks so they look isolated. For an alternative, the Horloge Fleurie on the quay gives a view of a stone beside the flower clock, and Quai Gustave-Ador shows the boulders rising from the water with the quay in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stones to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks washed out. Hold the phone steady with both hands or brace it on the railing when zoomed in, as zoom magnifies shake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the granite and the water. Quieter times of day make it easier to find a clear spot at the water's edge.

text.access_note: The stones are in open water and are seen from public lakeside spaces, with no paid viewpoint found; check the official site before you go if you plan anything beyond viewing from the shore.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late-afternoon light is usually softer and more flattering for the stones and water.
Quieter times of day make it easier to find a clear spot at the water's edge.
Zoomed phone shots are more affected by shake, and bracing on a railing helps.
A level horizon with gridlines gives a tidy composition.

name: Île Rousseau
label: Île Rousseau
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pont des Bergues' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pont des Bergues' (way/258441999): middle (204 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1083713: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Small island with a statue of Rousseau.

text.description:
Île Rousseau is a small island park in the middle of the Rhône in Geneva, named after the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau. A statue of him stands on the island, and a bridge links it to the shore. That makes it an easy, calm place to photograph. You get trees, water and a bit of city history in one frame.

A good place to photograph the island is the footbridge end of the Pont des Bergues, on the island side. From there you can see the island's tree-lined park, the Rhône flowing past, and the Jet d'Eau in view. The bridge is also the way onto the island, so the gateway itself makes a natural frame. Guides say the scene looks good by day and at night, so you can come back at a different hour for a different mood.

For a second angle, try the Pont du Mont-Blanc. From there the island is seen across the river, with the bridge in the foreground and the lake outflow behind it. It is only a brief suggestion, so treat it as an extra to try if you have time.

On your phone, keep the island as the main subject and let the water and trees fill the rest of the frame. Hold the phone steady against the bridge railing if you can. Once you have your shot of the island from the bridge, you can walk across and photograph the statue up close.
text.geographic_location: Île Rousseau sits in the middle of the Rhône in central Geneva, where the river leaves the lake. It is reached by a bridge from the shore, and the Pont des Bergues is the footbridge that leads onto it.
text.directions_text: From there the island is a very short walk away, about 1 minute on foot, to the north-east. Once you are on the island, you can walk around the park and find the statue of Rousseau. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the island, the river and the trees together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the bridge gateway in the foreground, and a little zoom (2x or more) to pick out the statue or the Jet d'Eau.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pont des Bergues (footbridge end on the island side). The island's tree-lined park and the Rhône with the Jet d'Eau in view, framed from the bridge that links to the island. The island lies to the north-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the island's trees along one of the lower lines, with the river leading into the frame. Include a little of the bridge railing or gateway in the foreground to give a sense of depth. For a different view, try the Pont du Mont-Blanc, where the island is seen across the river with the bridge in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the island's trees to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks too bright. In the evening, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides say the view looks good by day and at night, so choose whichever you prefer. Try both if you are staying nearby.

text.access_note: The island is a public park reached by a bridge, and no closures or restrictions were found, but check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Rhône leaves the lake at Geneva, near the island.
Resting your elbows on the bridge railing helps keep the phone still for night shots.
The Jet d'Eau appears in the distance from the footbridge end, and zoom of 2x or more can pick it out.

name: Russian Church, Geneva
label: Russian Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer and Rue François-Le-Fort (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/78492654: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Église Russe' (35 m across).

text.description: The Russian Church is a small Orthodox cathedral in the middle of one of Geneva's smart residential districts. Its full name is the Cathedral of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. It looks quite different from the apartment blocks around it, with gilded onion domes and a porch decorated in Byzantine-style stripes. That contrast is why it photographs so well: bright gold and patterned stonework against plain city streets. The church was designed by David Grimm of the Imperial Academy of Arts and finished in 1866. It was restored in 1966 and is still a working church today, so you will be photographing a building in daily use. The best-known view is from the corner of Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer, where the church sits on a small rise and you look straight at its front. From there the domes and the striped porch rise above the roofs of Les Tranchées. This is an exterior shot, so keep the whole building in the frame, then move closer for the details. Try one wide shot with some street in the foreground, one tighter shot of the domes, and one of the porch stripes. If you have time, the Promenade de l'Observatoire gives a different view, with the domes framed against the gardens and a wider outlook over the city.
text.geographic_location: The church is in Les Tranchées, a fashionable residential district of Geneva. It stands on a small rise on Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer, among apartment blocks.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Les Tranchées district and head for the corner of Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer. The church is to the north of it, about 1 minute on foot, so you can take your first photo before you walk up. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole front of the church. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the domes and porch stripes. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for when you are close and the street is narrow.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Rue Rodolphe-Toepffer and Rue François-Le-Fort (corner on the small rise, facing the church front). The gilded onion domes and striped porch rising above the surrounding apartment blocks of Les Tranchées.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the church centred, with the vertical lines straight so the building does not lean. Hold the phone level and keep the domes well inside the frame. For a different view, try the Promenade de l'Observatoire, where the domes are framed against the gardens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the golden domes to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold keeps its detail against a bright sky. If the sky is dull, a slight lift in exposure brings out the stripes on the porch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: On a clear day, choose a time when the sun is on the front of the church so the gold looks warm. Mid-morning or late afternoon is usually kinder than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The church is a working place of worship with limited opening hours and photography is not allowed inside, so stay outside for photos and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The gilded domes look best in direct sunlight, and mid-morning or late afternoon light is usually gentler than midday sun.
The street at the stand-here point is narrow enough that the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can help when you are close.

name: Paddle steamer Genève
label: Paddle steamer Genève
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Embarcadère du Mont-Blanc' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Parking du Mont-Blanc' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1474367300: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Genève' (64 m across).
notes: Belle Époque paddle steamer on Lake Geneva.

text.description: Genève is the oldest paddle ship on Lake Geneva. She was built in 1896 for the Compagnie Générale de Navigation sur le lac Léman and launched for the Swiss national exhibition in the city. Her steam engines were replaced with diesel in the 1930s, though the paddle-boat shape stayed. She was taken out of service in 1973 and later bought by a local association. She now lies moored at the Eaux-Vives dock, no longer sailing but still afloat. In the summer months she serves as a restaurant. She also has a sad place in history: in 1898 Empress Elisabeth of Bavaria was attacked just before boarding her, and the boat turned back to the Hôtel Beau-Rivage. The paddle boxes, long hull and tall funnel make her one of the more characterful subjects on the waterfront, and the lake behind her keeps a phone shot uncluttered. From there the boat sits along the shore to the east, with the lake on one side and the city waterfront on the other. She is fairly far from the pier, so use the telephoto lens to bring her closer rather than walking out of frame. Take one wider shot as well, so the quay, the water and the boat tell the story together. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines.
text.geographic_location: On the shore of Lake Geneva at the Eaux-Vives dock, a short way east of the Mont-Blanc landing stage along the lakefront. The Mont-Blanc pier is the nearest place to view her from.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Mont-Blanc landing on the lakefront in central Geneva, or come by taxi or hired scooter. The boat is about 5 minutes away, about 5 minutes on foot. For the photo itself you can stay on the pier and zoom in. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a scene-setting shot with the pier, lake and boat. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the hull and paddle boxes. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk right up to the boat, and watch for stretched edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Embarcadère du Mont-Blanc. The paddle steamer tied up at the Geneva harbour landing, seen from the quay with the lake and the city waterfront behind it. From there the paddle steamer is moored along the shore to the east, with the lake and the city waterfront around her. Turn to face east and keep the pier rail or edge out of the lower frame, or include it deliberately as a foreground line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the boat on a third of the frame with open water in front of her, and use the gridlines to keep the horizon straight. Take one tight telephoto shot of the funnel and paddle box, and one wide one with the quay and the city waterfront. If you are walking along the shore towards her, a closer shot with the ultra-wide lens can show the full length of the hull.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the boat to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the white paintwork keeps its detail. At 3x or 5x, hold the phone against the rail or tuck your elbows in to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives soft light on the boat when you face east, as the sun is behind you. Calm, still mornings give the cleanest reflections on the water.

text.access_note: The pier and lakeside promenade are public places, but check the official site before you go if you want to visit the boat itself or its summer restaurant.
